segments.narration: A mountain valley in Norway randomly produces floating, glowing fireballs. In Hessdalen, giant bright spheres hover silently over the snow, lasting for hours.
Radar tracked these mysterious lights accelerating to nineteen thousand miles per hour. Yet they made no sound and left no scorch marks.
How could a light show move faster than a missile without a sonic boom? For decades, science was stumped.
The answer lay in the dirt: copper and zinc rocks on opposing riverbanks created a giant natural battery in the water.
This natural circuit charges the air, igniting gas into floating plasma spheres right before your eyes.

verdicts.claim: Glowing unexplained light spheres have been frequently observed over the Hessdalen valley in Norway.
verdicts.note: The reference articles confirm that unidentified, floating, and hovering lights of various colors have been observed in the Hessdalen valley in rural central Norway since at least the 1930s.

verdicts.claim: Radar measurements in Hessdalen recorded anomalous light phenomena traveling at speeds reaching up to thirty thousand kilometers per hour.
verdicts.note: The reference text notes estimated light ball velocities of up to 20,000 m/s, but does not explicitly mention radar measurements or thirty thousand kilometers per hour.

verdicts.claim: Scientific field research into the Hessdalen lights began in the early 1980s.
verdicts.note: The reference text confirms that Project Hessdalen initiated field investigations to scientific investigate the lights starting in 1983.

verdicts.claim: Geological analysis of Hessdalen revealed copper deposits on one side of the valley and iron or zinc deposits on the other, separated by a river.
verdicts.note: The text describes a geological battery model where the two sides of the valley act as electrodes and the river Hesja acts as the electrolyte, but it does not specify copper, iron, or zinc deposits.

verdicts.claim: A leading scientific model explains the Hessdalen lights as glowing plasma generated by natural battery-like geological conditions.
verdicts.note: The text references Jader Monari's 2014 geological battery model where river electrolyte and valley electrodes electrically charge rising gas bubbles, alongside plasma models explaining the luminescent phenomenon.
